idiom_name: frozen snapshot + Thread::Mutex-guarded replace (dup/merge/freeze); MRI's internal sharing stays in the VM
implementation_notes: Ruby's copy-on-write lives inside the interpreter - MRI shares string buffers and duplicated objects are shallow by design - and Ruby threads share the whole object graph under the GVL, so the pattern is written as a frozen snapshot plus a guarded replace: read the current frozen object without a lock, build the next version with dup/merge/select, freeze it, and swap the reference while holding a Thread::Mutex, which is documented as 'a simple semaphore that can be used to coordinate access to shared data from multiple concurrent threads'. The reference count itself is nothing a Ruby program should write: the VM owns it, and there is no deterministic free. The classic counted-body handle is justified only when binding to a C extension that hands you one.
pitfalls: freeze is shallow: a frozen Hash whose values are mutable Arrays still changes underneath its readers - freeze the values too (Ractor.make_shareable when deep sharing is needed); a FrozenError only protects the object you froze, not what it points at.

The GVL hides races instead of preventing them: a check-then-act sequence across a snapshot (read, compute, replace) still loses updates unless the whole sequence holds the Mutex, and on JRuby or TruffleRuby (no GVL) even a single-property publication needs the lock or a concurrent collection.

Copies are shallow and sized by the data: Hash#merge/#dup copy one level, so nested state is shared with every earlier snapshot, and MRI's shared-string optimisation means a dup'd String may keep sharing its buffer until the first write - a 'cheap copy' that becomes a hidden full copy later.
sources: Ruby 3.4 documentation, Thread::Mutex - 'Mutex implements a simple semaphore that can be used to coordinate access to shared data from multiple concurrent threads': https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/3.4/Thread/Mutex.html

Ruby 3.4 documentation, Ractor - Ractor 'is designed to provide a parallel execution feature of Ruby without thread-safety concerns', i.e. by not sharing the object graph at all: https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/3.4/ractor_md.html
